Practice point: Always lay s.3 as an alternative to s.15. If purpose fails, possession remains.

7.4 Section 15A — sale or supply, value €13,000 or more
•   Proofs: s.15 proofs plus market value (or aggregate) of €13,000 or more at any time while in
possession; proved beyond reasonable doubt; DPP consent (s.15A(4)). Indictment only.
•   Market value = the price the drug could be expected to fetch on the illicit market (s.15A(5)). Witness:
a Garda or customs officer the court is satisfied has knowledge of unlawful sale or supply (s.15A(3)).
•   No mens rea as to value (s.15A(3A); Power [2007] IESC 31).
People (DPP) v Connolly [2011] IESC 6
Facts: About 10kg of amphetamine in ten bags. A Garda valued it at €145,755 (€15,000/kg) assuming at
least 10% purity. The FSI scientist tested five bags qualitatively and said purities "generally" fall between
10% and 40%; she agreed 1% would trigger her test.
Held: Value is an essential ingredient to be proved beyond reasonable doubt. "Generally" left open cases
outside the range; probability is not enough. The case should have been withdrawn; conviction set aside;
no retrial.
Lesson: Where valuation assumes a purity floor, get quantitative analysis — or value in a way that does
not depend on purity. The risk is greatest near the threshold; in Rattigan the trial court found purity had
"little or no bearing" because the value exceeded €13,000 by an enormous factor.

People (DPP) v Power [2007] IESC 31
Held: Reading ss.15, 15A and 29 together as one code, it would be absurd to require knowledge of value
when knowledge that the package contained drugs need not be proved. No mens rea as to value.

Model charge — s.15A
…did have in your possession, for the purpose of selling or otherwise supplying to
another in contravention of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2017, a controlled drug,
to wit cocaine, the market value of which amounted to €13,000 or more, contrary to
section 15A and section 27 (as amended) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1977.

Do this: Indictment: s.15A, s.15, s.3. Value statement: experience and sources; FSI net weight and purity;
unit price and market level with reasons; calculation; confirmation that the most conservative price still
exceeds €13,000. Record the DPP consent.

7.5 Section 15B — importation, value €13,000 or more
•   Import in contravention of the Regulations; value at or about the time of importation €13,000+; value
witness (s.15B(2)); no knowledge of value needed (s.15B(3)); DPP consent (s.15B(4)); same
sentencing regime as s.15A.

•   Lower-value importation: s.21(2) with the import regulation (14 years), plus Customs Act offences.
•   Document the statutory power for every step of a parcel interception (Lawel [2014] IECCA 33, Part
3.7).

7.6 Section 15C — drugs into prisons and places of detention
• Offences: (a) convey a controlled drug into a prison, children detention school or remand centre or to
a person there; (b) place a drug inside or outside with intent it reach a person there; (c) throw or
project a drug in; (d) possess a drug in the vicinity with intent to do (a)–(c).
• Any quantity (s.15C(2)); no need to prove an intended recipient (s.15C(4)); presumption of intent for
(d) from proximity, packaging and time (s.15C(3)); prison officer search power (s.15C(5)).
• Penalty: summary Class B fine and/or 12 months; indictment fine and/or 10 years.
Practice point: Drone and throw-over drops: preserve the packaging, record distance from the wall, time,
and any phone contact with inmates; charge (c) and (d) together where appropriate.

7.9 Section 20 and section 21
•   s.20: aiding, abetting, counselling or inducing an offence outside the State under a "corresponding
law"; foreign government certificate is evidence of the law and the offence (s.20(2)–(3)). 14 years.
•   s.21(1): attempt; aid, abet, counsel, procure; solicit or incite — punished as the substantive offence
(s.27(5)).

•     s.21(2): contravening the Regulations — the vehicle for actual supply, offering to supply,
import/export and manufacture. "Offering to supply" is complete on the offer; messages offering
drugs are strong evidence. Regulations under s.5(1)(a) (other than transportation): summary Class C
and/or 12 months, indictment 14 years; other regulations or transportation: summary Class C and/or 6
months, indictment 2 years (s.27(6)).
•     s.21(3)–(7): false information under Regulations; obstructing a Garda exercising an MDA power
(s.21(4) — swallowing or discarding drugs during a lawful search; continuing offence possible);

Part 8 — Evidence: Continuity, Experts, Devices, Hearsay,
Disclosure
8.1 Continuity and the FSI certificate
A certificate purporting to be signed by an officer of Forensic Science Ireland is evidence of the matters
stated (s.10 Misuse of Drugs Act 1984, as substituted by s.170 of the Criminal Justice (Forensic Evidence
and DNA Database System) Act 2014). Continuity connects that certificate to what you seized.
Ratinskis v Director of Public Prosecutions [2026] IESC 33 (11 June 2026)
Facts: Drink-driving prosecution on a blood specimen. The doctor divided the sample into two sealed,
numbered containers; the Garda completed the s.15 Road Traffic Act 2010 form, offered one container to
the accused, sealed the other in a box and posted it to the Medical Bureau of Road Safety the next day.
No evidence was given of where the box was kept overnight. The High Court (Phelan J, 31 July 2025)
quashed the conviction for a gap in the chain of custody, relying on A McD, halting prosecutions
nationally.
Held: Leapfrog appeal allowed. There is no general rule of law requiring proof of a chain of custody for
real evidence as a condition of admissibility; A McD said only that the party adducing evidence "must be
able" to account for its custody — a matter of weight for the fact-finder. The specimen is not itself
evidence; the statutory certificate is, and it is admissible if duly completed. The prosecution need not
exclude every hypothetical possibility. (The Court also said the issue was for a case stated, not judicial
review.)
Lesson: Continuity failures are not automatically fatal — but they go to weight, and in a contested drugs
trial weight is decided by a jury who will hear every gap. The 2026 decision is a safety net, not a licence.

People (DPP) v A McD [2016] IESC 71 — CCTV is real evidence, not hearsay; operation of the system
need not be proved as a precondition, but the party adducing it must be able to account for its custody if
reliability is questioned.
Do this: Seal at scene in tamper-evident bags; record seal numbers; one bag per location and suspect;
sign and time every transfer; PULSE property entries; FSI submission lists seal numbers and the analysis
required (identification, net weight, quantification where value is purity-sensitive); fingerprint/DNA on
packaging requested before drug analysis; on return, check seals and note condition.

8.2 Expert and opinion evidence
•   Value (s.15A(3)/15B(2)): the court must first be satisfied the witness has knowledge of unlawful sale
and supply. Lay the foundation: unit, years, seizures, valuations, sources of price data.
•   Drug language and records: in Rattigan a Sergeant interpreted "dark" as heroin and a list as a tick
list; the appeal contested his expertise. Establish experience and basis before interpreting language or
ledgers.
•   Separate fact from opinion in statements; disclose the basis of every opinion.

8.3 Phones, data and attribution
•   Attribution chain: where the handset was found and by whom; SIM(s); subscriber or top-up records;
contacts saved under the accused’s name; use by the accused (photos, messages signed, calls to
family); CCTV of the phone in hand (Rattigan); extraction report and timestamps.
•   Retained data: judicial authorisation under the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011 as
amended in 2022 (Dwyer, CJEU C-140/20). Apply early.
•   Device content: specific authority in the information (Quirke); further warrant before examination if
not.
•   Encrypted platforms and foreign data: mutual legal assistance (2008 Act); expect admissibility
challenges; document every link.

8.4 Hearsay — intelligence before the jury
People (DPP) v Noonan [2024] IECA 275
Facts: Car stopped on the N7 by ANPR (no tax); no insurance or licence; car seized. At the compound
the member found amphetamine and alprazolam worth €137,858 in the boot. At trial the member told the

jury of a call from an Inspector who said he had confidential information that a large quantity of drugs was
in that car; the Inspector did not testify. The accused denied knowledge.
Held: Hearsay admitted as a plank of the prosecution case; significant prejudice and unfairness to the
defence. s.15A conviction (9 years) quashed; retrial ordered.
Lesson: Grounds for a search go to the judge on a voir dire if lawfulness is disputed. The content of
intelligence never goes before the jury.

8.5 Controlled deliveries and entrapment
•   Cross-border controlled deliveries: Criminal Justice (Mutual Assistance) Act 2008, ss.88–90; drugs
importations run under the Garda–Customs Memorandum of Understanding and operational protocol
(s.90(4)).
• Record the legal power for interception, examination, detention, seizure and delivery (Lawel [2014]
IECCA 33). Capture what the recipient did (Lawel [2017] IECA 253: signed as "Tony Tutu", handed
keys to a co-accused who removed the parcel 15 minutes later).
• Ireland has no substantive entrapment defence; the remedy is exclusion or a stay where the State
incited an offence that would not otherwise have been committed.
Teixeira de Castro v Portugal (1998) 28 EHRR 101 — Article 6 breached where undercover officers
incited a sale by a person with no predisposition.
Ramanauskas v Lithuania ECtHR [GC], 5 February 2008 — Incitement test; passive investigation
permissible.
R v Looseley [2001] UKHL 53 — persuasive — An unexceptional opportunity is legitimate; luring or
pressure is not.

8.6 Lost evidence, CCTV and disclosure
Braddish v DPP [2001] 3 IR 127 — Prosecution prohibited where Gardaí lost the video on which the
identification rested.
Dunne v DPP [2002] 2 IR 305 — Duty to seek out and preserve CCTV bearing on guilt or innocence.
Savage v DPP [2008] IESC 39 — The accused must show a real risk of an unfair trial that directions
cannot cure, engaging with what the missing evidence would realistically show.
•   Disclose material that could assist the defence or undermine the prosecution; schedule unused
material.
•   Informer privilege protects source identity but yields where disclosure is necessary to show innocence;
the trial judge may inspect. Never put source details in a statement.
•   A co-accused’s out-of-court statement is evidence only against its maker; accomplice evidence needs
the corroboration warning — plan independent corroboration (phones, surveillance, money).

Part 9 — Charging, Procedure and Diversion
9.1 Decision pathway
1. Adult, first drug offence, small amount for personal use? Assess for the Health Referral Scheme
(below).
2. Adult, s.3 cannabis, not eligible or already referred? Consider the Adult Caution Scheme.
3. Under 18? Children Act 2001, Part 4 (Garda Youth Diversion). The s.27(3C) minimum never applies to
under-18s. Consider the 2024 Act against any adult who used the child.
4. Summary disposal? Charge or summons; Gardaí prosecute in the DPP’s name under general
directions.
5. Indictable or doubtful? File to DPP for directions. s.15A and s.15B always require DPP consent to
institute proceedings.

9.2 Health Referral Scheme (in force 1 September 2026)
• A Garda alternative to prosecution: referral of an eligible adult found with a small quantity of any
controlled drug for personal use to the HSE for a brief health intervention. A key deliverable of the
National Drugs Strategy 2026–2029. Possession remains an offence under s.3.
• Eligibility: 18+; first drug offence (no previous drug conviction or adult caution); admits possession for
personal use at the time; willing to participate. No fixed quantities — judged on the circumstances.
• Decision: investigating Garda and Superintendent (or Inspector acting). Refusal must be reasoned
and recorded; the person may seek review by a different Superintendent/Inspector.
• Process: person told immediately they will be considered; contacted by the means given; attends a
station to accept; non-attendance → prosecution. Offered once only. Recorded on PULSE; not a
conviction; not disclosed for vetting; may be disclosed to a court on request.
Where Gardaí go wrong: Not recording the assessment; not preserving the drugs and admission
because "it’s going to HRS" — then the person never attends and there is no prosecutable file.
Do this: Caution, record the admission, seize and submit the drugs as normal, record the decision and
reasons, diary the acceptance deadline.

Part 10 — Sentencing, Garda Sentencing Evidence and
Ancillary Orders
10.1 Ranges and method
People (DPP) v Samuilis [2018] IECA 316
Held: For s.15 and s.15A the effective maximum in most cases is about 15 years: low 0–5; mid 5–10;
upper 10–15. Grow-house tiers: organisers/funders (high); managers (mid); gardeners, often exploited or
trafficked (low). Where s.15A is charged, assess the headline without reference to the presumptive
minimum, apply mitigation, and only if the result is below 10 years ask whether exceptional and specific
circumstances make the minimum unjust.

People (DPP) v Sarsfield [2019] IECA 260
Held: Survey of appellate s.15A sentences: values over €1m averaged about 9 years with part
suspended; average effective sentence about 6¾ years (treated with caution). High-level commercial
dealing in very large quantities: headline of the order of 14–15 years, sometimes significantly higher. A
plea alone is unlikely to justify going below the minimum in very high-end cases, especially on
overwhelming evidence.

People (DPP) v O’Mahony and Brennan [2014] IECA 57 — €3.5m cocaine and heroin; early pleas; no
previous convictions; addiction addressed. 13 years with 3 suspended upheld.
People (DPP) v Kilkenny [2016] IECA 348 — Grow house, potential value €2.8m: organiser increased on
review from 10 years (6 suspended) to 12 (4 suspended); gardeners 7 years with 6 suspended. Roles
must be differentiated.
People (DPP) v Bogdan [2016] IECA 70 — Knowing importation of €1.5m of cannabis herb for €5,000: 6
years not disturbed.

10.2 The prosecuting Garda at the sentencing hearing
People (DPP) v Lawel [2017] IECA 253
Facts: Plea to s.15A after a controlled delivery of €1.4m of cocaine to the accused’s house, signed for as
"Tony Tutu" (a fictitious South African consul) and collected by a co-accused 15 minutes later; the
accused got €20 for diesel. In evidence the prosecuting Garda accepted that the accused did not know
the parcel contained drugs (only that it was illegal), was vulnerable to the co-accused, was on the lowest
rung, had no role in organisation or distribution, co-operated fully and materially assisted, and was
unlikely to reoffend. Sentence: 10 years with 3 suspended — the co-accused organisers got 10 years
unsuspended.
Held: The 30% reduction left about 5% for everything beyond the plea (which alone would justify roughly
25%). Error in principle; resentenced to 6 years with the final 18 months suspended. The Court called the
Garda’s acceptance that the accused did not know he was handling drugs "quite exceptional".
Lesson: Your concessions in the witness box shape the sentence. Give them only when they are true
and supported by the file.

Do this: Prepare a sentencing note: role and the evidence for it; what was admitted and when; what the
accused did not assist with; previous convictions; value, quantity and purity; aggravating features
(children, weapons, prison, violence, proximity to schools); assets and cash seized; any trafficking
indicators. Answer only from that note.

10.3 The s.27 regime for s.15A and s.15B
•   Life maximum; the court must specify a minimum of 10 years unless exceptional and specific
circumstances make that unjust (s.27(3C)–(3D)), having regard in particular to the plea (stage and
circumstances) and material assistance, and to any previous drug trafficking conviction and the public
interest in preventing trafficking.
•   Not applicable to under-18s. Remission applies (s.27(3H)). Commutation/remission and temporary
release restricted during the minimum term (s.27(3G), (3I)). Addiction review after at least half the
minimum term (s.27(3J)–(3K)). No parole eligibility during a specified minimum term (Parole Act 2019,
s.24(12)).

McManus v Minister for Justice and Equality [2021] IEHC 385
Facts: A repeat s.15A offender was sentenced to 15 years with 3 suspended under s.27(3F), which
mandated 10 years for a second or subsequent s.15A/15B offence.
Held: Following Ellis v Minister for Justice [2019] IESC 30 (an identical Firearms Act provision), s.27(3F)
applied a mandatory minimum only to a limited class defined by prior conviction and breached Article
34.1 (separation of powers). Declaration granted; sentence quashed and remitted. Finalised sentences
are not reopened (A v Governor of Arbour Hill Prison [2006] 4 IR 88).
Now: Repeat offenders are sentenced under s.27(3C)–(3D); the previous conviction is aggravating
(s.27(3B)) and counts against departure (s.27(3D)(c)). Cross-references removed by the Criminal Justice
(Amendment) Act 2021, s.6.

10.4 Forfeiture, confiscation, cash and assets
Bowes v Devally [1995] 2 ILRM 148 (HC, Geoghegan J)
Facts: Conviction for s.3 possession of a small amount of cannabis resin. £890 in the same room bore
traces of cannabis; the accused said she was minding it for her mother. The District and Circuit Courts
ordered forfeiture under s.30.
Held: Forfeiture is part of the penalty and strictly construed: the property must relate to the offence of
conviction. Even if intended to buy more drugs, the cash had nothing to do with simple possession. Order
quashed and remitted. It would differ on a supply conviction where the money might be proceeds.
